title: Bidirectional BFS in San Francisco: Meet-in-Middle ⚡
description: Watch two BFS searches start from opposite ends on a real city grid and stop the moment they meet. This “meeting in the middle” bidirectional approach slashes the explored space and makes shortest-path routing feel instant.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — How launching two simultaneous searches doubles graph traversal speed ⚡

In this SoMa map, we run BFS from the start and from the goal at the same time. Instead of exploring outward from one side (classic BFS), each frontier expands level-by-level until a node appears in both visited sets. The first intersection gives the shortest path, but with dramatically fewer expansions—especially on large, branching graphs.

🔧 What’s happening (the “coding interview prep” version):
• Maintain two queues: qF (from start) and qB (from goal)
• Maintain two visited maps/sets: seenF, seenB (optionally parents to reconstruct the path)
• Expand the smaller frontier each step (optional optimization)
• When a neighbor is in the other side’s visited set, you’ve found the meeting point

✅ Takeaway: bidirectional bfs explained in one line—same shortest guarantee, less work, because the search radius shrinks from exploring depth d to roughly d/2 from each direction.

Debate question: In practice, is “expand the smaller frontier” the real performance winner, or is it the bidirectional structure itself?
